title: Duration, Modified Duration and Convexity
objectives: Compute Macaulay duration as the present-value-weighted average time of a bond's cash flows
Convert Macaulay to modified duration and use it to estimate price changes for small yield moves
Compute convexity and apply the second-order correction to price estimates
Explain why duration-only estimates undershoot fully repriced bond values
motivation: You run \$250 million of 10-year bonds. Rates move 10 basis points while you read this paragraph, did the book just gain or lose five figures? Duration answers instantly; convexity repairs the error duration leaves behind. We build both from first principles on a small 3-year bond, compare the duration estimate against a full repricing, and watch the convexity term close the gap to under a cent.

blocks.md: A price is a snapshot; a risk number is a slope. Since the price $P(y)$ is a smooth, decreasing function of yield, the first question a risk manager asks is how fast it falls: for a small move $\Delta y$, the percentage price change is approximately $-D_{\text{mod}}\,\Delta y$. This lesson defines that slope precisely, computes it two ways, as a cash-flow-weighted time and as a derivative, and then measures how much the straight-line estimate misses. The miss is systematic and its size is measurable, which is exactly where convexity enters.

blocks.caption: First order: modified duration. Second order: convexity $C$.

blocks.text: Macaulay duration: time weighted by money

blocks.md: Macaulay duration is the average time until the bond's cash flows arrive, weighted by the present value of each flow: $D_{\text{Mac}} = \sum_t t\,w_t$ with $w_t = \text{PV}(C_t)/P$. A zero-coupon bond pays everything at maturity, so its Macaulay duration equals its maturity exactly; coupons pull the average earlier. Duration doubles as the sensitivity lever once you adjust for compounding: with annual coupons, modified duration is $D_{\text{mod}} = D_{\text{Mac}}/(1+y)$, the percentage price change per unit change in yield.

blocks.title: Macaulay duration of the 3-year, 5% coupon bond at 6% (price \$973.27)
items: Macaulay duration $\approx 2.857$ years, close to maturity because 90% of the value arrives at year 3.
Modified duration: $2.857 / 1.06 = 2.696$ - the bond moves about 2.7% per 100 bp yield change.

blocks.title: Duration estimate vs full repricing, yields +100 bp
items: The straight-line estimate is \$0.48 too low, and duration always undershoots the new price after a move, because the true price-yield curve bows away from its tangent.

blocks.caption: Annual-pay convexity: the dispersion of cash flows around the duration, scaled by the compounding factor.

blocks.title: Convexity of the same bond
items: Correction for a 100 bp move: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10.00 \times (0.01)^2 = 0.0005$, i.e. +0.05% of price = +\$0.49.
Corrected estimate: $947.03 + 0.49 = \$947.52$ against the actual \$947.51, the error is now under a cent.

blocks.title: Convexity is a gift to holders
blocks.md: Positive convexity means the price falls less than duration predicts when yields rise and rises more when yields fall: for a long-only holder it is free insurance. Options embedded in callable bonds and mortgages sell that insurance away, producing negative convexity near the call price, which is why callable paper cheapens in yield terms.

blocks.title: Keep the conventions straight
blocks.md: Macaulay duration is in years; modified duration is percent per unit of yield. With continuous compounding the two coincide; with annual compounding divide by $(1+y)$; with semiannual coupons divide by $(1 + y/2)$. Mixing conventions misstates risk by several percent instantly.

blocks.caption: Shift the whole curve in one parallel move and compare the duration estimate against the repriced bond, the widening gap is the convexity term at work.

blocks.code:
cfs = {1: 50, 2: 50, 3: 1050}
y, price = 0.06, 973.2699
pv = {t: c / (1 + y) ** t for t, c in cfs.items()}
mac = sum(t * v for t, v in pv.items()) / price
mod = mac / (1 + y)
conv = sum(t * (t + 1) * v for t, v in pv.items()) / (price * (1 + y) ** 2)
print(round(mac, 3), round(mod, 3), round(conv, 2))
# 2.857 2.696 10.0
blocks.caption: The three risk numbers of the worked bond, reproduced exactly.

blocks.md: Duration is the answer to the question every bond desk asks first: *if rates move 1%, how much money do I make or lose?* The naive answer. "it depends on the coupon and maturity", is correct and useless. Duration compresses coupon, maturity and yield into one slope number, and convexity reports the curvature that the slope misses. Both are approximations to the bond's true price function, and knowing when the approximation breaks is the actual skill.

blocks.title: Full worked example: a 3-year 4% annual-coupon bond at par
items: The bond pays \$4, \$4, \$104 at years 1, 2, 3 and yields $4\%$, so it prices exactly at par: $P = \frac{4}{1.04} + \frac{4}{1.04^2} + \frac{104}{1.04^3} = \$100.00.
Macaulay duration weights each payment time by present value: $D_{mac} = \frac{1\cdot3.846 + 2\cdot3.698 + 3\cdot92.455}{100} = 2.886$ years.
Modified duration: $D_{mod} = \frac{2.886}{1.04} = 2.775$. The headline sensitivity: $\Delta P \approx -D_{mod} \cdot P \cdot \Delta y$, so $+1\%$ in yield predicts roughly $-\$2.78 on a \$100 bond.
Reality check, reprice exactly at $5\%$: the true price is \$97.2768, a fall of \$2.7232. The duration-only estimate said \$2.7751: an error of about 5 cents.

Add convexity $C = 10.53$: $\Delta P \approx -D_{mod}P\Delta y + \tfrac{1}{2}CP(\Delta y)^2$ predicts \$97.2776, so the error drops below one-tenth of a cent. At $\pm 1\%$ the convexity term is worth roughly 5 cents; at $\pm 3\%$ it is worth almost half a dollar.

blocks.md: Why the errors are asymmetric: a bond's price is **convex** in yield, it falls less than duration predicts when yields rise, and rises more when yields fall. Long-dated and low-coupon bonds have the most curvature, which is why convexity is reported next to duration for anything beyond a short book. The same second-order thinking reappears in gamma for options: first-order Greeks tell you the slope, the cross-Greek tells you how the slope itself moves.

blocks.title: Duration is a tangent line, not the curve
blocks.md: Every duration number is a local derivative computed at today's yield. After a $2\%$ move, the slope itself has changed, the hedge ratio you computed this morning is stale this afternoon. Books with material convexity re-strike hedges as rates move; the frequency of that rebalancing is a risk decision, not a technicality.

guidedExercise.prompt: A 2-year bond pays a 10% annual coupon on \$1{,}000 face and yields 10%, so it prices at par (\$1,000). Compute its Macaulay duration and modified duration, and explain why the duration is below the maturity.
hints: PV of year-1 coupon: 100/1.10. PV of year-2 flow: 1100/1.10^2.
Weights are each PV divided by 1000.
guidedExercise.solution: PVs: $100/1.10 = 90.9091$ and $1100/1.10^2 = 1100/1.21 = 909.0909$ (they sum to 1000, the par price). $D_{\text{Mac}} = (1 \times 90.9091 + 2 \times 909.0909)/1000 = 1909.0909/1000 = 1.9091$ years. $D_{\text{mod}} = 1.9091/1.10 = 1.7355$. Duration sits below the 2-year maturity because the year-1 coupon pulls the average arrival time earlier.

independentExercise.prompt: The 4-year, 6% coupon bond from the previous lesson (yield 7%, price \$966.13) has cash-flow PVs of 56.0748, 52.4063, 48.9779 and 808.6690 for years 1-4. Compute its Macaulay duration, modified duration, and the duration-based price estimate for a +50 bp parallel move.
hints: Weight each PV by its year and divide the sum by 966.13.
Estimate: delta P = -D_mod x 0.005 x price.

commonMistakes: Quoting Macaulay duration as a percentage price sensitivity, that is modified duration's job.
Dividing by $(1+y)$ when the bond pays semiannual coupons (use $1 + y/2$).
Applying the duration estimate to large moves without the convexity term, errors grow with $(\Delta y)^2$.
Adding durations of positions without first scaling by market value, risk adds in dollars, not in years.
realWorldApplication: Asset-liability managers match portfolio duration to liability duration to immunize funded status; immunization works precisely because duration translates parallel yield moves into offsetting value changes.
quantFinanceApplication: Duration and convexity are the first two terms of a Taylor expansion of the pricing function, the same expansion that produces delta-gamma option PnL approximations later in the options track.
summary: Duration converts yield moves into price moves: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{\text{mod}}\,\Delta y$.
Macaulay duration is the PV-weighted average time to a bond's cash flows; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity.
Modified duration divides Macaulay by $(1+y)$ for annual compounding; they coincide under continuous compounding.
Convexity adds $\tfrac{1}{2}C(\Delta y)^2$; on the worked bond it cut a \$0.48 error to under a cent on a 100 bp move.
Convexity helps holders: prices fall less than the tangent predicts and rise more.

quiz.prompt: What is the Macaulay duration of a 5-year zero-coupon bond (annual compounding)?
quiz.explanation: All value arrives at maturity, so the PV-weighted average time is exactly 5 years. For zeros, duration = maturity.

quiz.prompt: What is the modified duration of that 5-year zero at a 6% annual yield? (Two decimals.)
Which bond has the highest duration?
options: A 10-year bond with an 8% annual coupon
A 3-year bond with a 10% annual coupon
quiz.explanation: Longest maturity and lowest (zero) coupon both push duration up: the 10-year zero has all its weight at year 10.

quiz.prompt: A bond has modified duration 7.2. Estimate the percentage price change for a +25 bp parallel shift. (Include the sign.)

options: The price rises more when yields fall than it falls when yields rise by the same amount
Duration stays constant at all yield levels
Convexity applies only to zero-coupon bonds
quiz.explanation: The price-yield curve bows above its tangent, so the linear duration estimate undershoots the new price on both up and down moves. That asymmetry favors holders.

options: Macaulay duration is the PV-weighted average time to receive the bond's cash flows
Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + y) for annual compounding
Duration falls as the bond's maturity shortens
quiz.explanation: Higher coupons push more value to earlier years, lowering duration, so statement 3 is wrong. The others are standard definitions.

flashcards.back: $D_{\text{Mac}} = \sum_t t \cdot \text{PV}(C_t)/P$ - the PV-weighted average time to cash flows, in years.
$D_{\text{mod}} = D_{\text{Mac}}/(1+y)$ (annual compounding); approximates % price change per unit yield change.
Equals its maturity, all cash arrives at one date. Coupons shorten duration; higher yields also shorten it.
